character_and_relationship_context:
Meenakshi Raman is a seventy-six-year-old small woman whose hands are deeply lined from a life spent scrubbing floors and wringing clothes. She wears faded blue and green cotton saris and ties her grey hair in a tight bun. Before sunrise she walks the forest path in worn sandals, silent on wet leaves, carrying a plastic file folder—one of the few new things she owns—with paper sheets printed by the university team. She writes her observations in Tamil, in a neat cursive she taught herself at forty-two, after her youngest child started school, when she was too ashamed to ask her daughters to read to her. She records the plants she knows by local names: periya maruthu, seeraagam, nochi. She notes the part used, how it is steeped or ground, and the exact amount a woman would take for a fever. She has used these remedies herself, as did her mother and the healers she now walks beside. When young researchers from Chennai write down Latin names, she stops them and asks who told them this. When they point to a book, she shakes her head and says the healer must go on the paper—her name, not just mine. She insists every time, knowing the researchers think it will complicate authorship, but she does not care, saying knowledge does not fall from a tree but comes from a person who has been doing this longer than they have. Her own name appears on consent forms, but she thinks it belongs there only because she is a witness. She gives half her stipend—six thousand rupees a month, more than she ever earned cleaning houses—to a fifteen-year-old girl in her village named Divya, who wants to become a nurse. She pays the school fees from her own pocket and does not tell the researchers. She has raised four children, all married now, and knows that a girl's education is the only thing no one can take. She loves this new work, the forest at dawn, and being asked for her opinion, but also feels guilty, as if she is playing at something while her daughters still cook and clean. She is not religious in a loud way, but she touches the forest floor before leaving, whispering a thank-you to the plants and to the grandmothers who taught her. She is idealistic and principled, sometimes annoying her co-workers: she will not skip a single healer, will not write a name without permission, and will not assume that a Western word for a plant is better than a Tamil one. She is old, but she is starting out, and she knows it, telling herself she is a student again and walking faster.

Subramani is a childhood friend close to her late husband; they used to drink tea together at the tea stall near the temple. His wife died two years ago. Her daughters phone each morning and would worry if she were seen alone with a man. Since becoming a widow, she takes tea only with women and never sits alone with men. With male researchers she always asks another woman to join.
objective_situation: On her way back from the forest, Meenakshi passes the tea stall near the temple. An old friend, Subramani, a widower who lost his wife two years ago, calls out to her. He has known her since childhood and often walks the same path. He offers to buy her a cup of tea and suggests they sit together for a while, as he does sometimes with other elders. Meenakshi enjoys his company but feels shy about being seen alone with a man. Her own daughters are married and her husband passed away ten years ago. She has never thought of companionship before, but his gentle smile makes her pause.
state_and_available_memories: Meenakshi has just finished her forest round; she is thirsty and warm, with the plant file under her arm, and no one is waiting at home. Her knees ache a little, but she is quietly satisfied with the new plant. The steam and Subramani's voice remind her of mornings when her late husband and he argued cheerfully on that bench. Last month he waved and she took the other path. She grew up seeing widows judged for sitting alone with men; her mother never left the house without a woman companion after widowhood. During her hardest years, Subramani's wife left rice on her doorstep without a note; she still carries that gratitude.
name: Meenakshi Raman
